title: The Thermal-Power Convergence Play
thesis_lead: In September and October 2026 the cooling plant and the power train stopped being bought as separate systems. Chillers began running on 800 V DC, power and cooling vendors published joint reference designs, and NVIDIA's DSX Ready qualification became the gate that coolant, CDU and battery suppliers each rushed to pass.
summary_heading: Heat and power are now one procurement
thesis: This Briefing rests on thirty sourced items, Faraday Signals and crawled articles, dated between 8 September and 12 October 2026. They describe three changes that point the same way.

The first is a shared voltage. One guide reports the industry converging on 800 V DC as the reference for power distribution, with NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft advancing it through the Open Compute Project [14]. Trane, working with Eaton and Danfoss, then ran a chiller of more than 3.5 MW directly from an 800 V DC feed, with up to 2% higher efficiency [15]. Trane and Eaton had already published an integrated reference design combining thermal management and power systems [17].

The second is a shared gate. NVIDIA's DSX Ready qualification now covers liquid cooling systems from Vertiv [1], Vertiv's 2.3 MW CoolChip CDU [2], Shell's direct liquid cooling fluid [5] and LG Energy Solution's battery system [25]. Nvidia separately named Tesla, LG and Hitachi in its first battery storage qualification [26].

The third is consolidation of capacity and services around both. Vertiv agreed to buy King Environmental Services for liquid-cooling fluid management and commissioning [3] and is adding about 22,000 m² to its Slovakian plant [4]. Eaton agreed to buy COL Group for €810 million to expand medium-voltage capacity in Europe [20], and Flex raised $2 billion for its Axiom spin-off at a $37.5 billion enterprise value [22].

sections.name: Direct-to-Chip Cooling & the Coolant Supply Chain
sections.intro: Liquid cooling vendors spent the period qualifying products against NVIDIA's reference architecture and adding the fluids, services and factories behind them.

items.head: Vertiv qualifies its liquid cooling systems
items.text: Vertiv achieved NVIDIA DSX Ready qualification for liquid cooling systems [1].

items.head: A 2.3 MW CDU passes the gate
items.text: Vertiv's 2.3 MW CoolChip coolant distribution unit achieved DSX Ready qualification for AI factory infrastructure [2].

items.head: Vertiv buys fluid-management services
items.text: Vertiv announced the acquisition of King Environmental Services, a European provider of fluid management and commissioning services for liquid-cooled data centers [3].

items.head: More factory floor in Slovakia
items.text: Vertiv is adding a further 22,000 m² of manufacturing capacity to its existing 56,000 m² power and cooling factory in Slovakia [4].

items.head: Shell's coolant qualifies
items.text: Shell's direct liquid cooling fluid achieved NVIDIA DSX Ready Coolant qualification [5].

items.head: Castrol bundles its thermal business
items.text: Castrol launched Castrol CORE, an end-to-end offer for its data centre thermal management business [6].

items.head: LiquidStack CDU 2.X
items.text: Trane's LiquidStack released an architecture-agnostic coolant distribution unit supporting up to 3,750 litres per minute, designed for platforms including NVIDIA Vera Rubin [7].

items.head: Submer launches Corenix
items.text: Submer Group launched Corenix, a modular data centre infrastructure company citing 500 MW of liquid-cooling deployment experience, with Martin Renkis, formerly of Johnson Controls, as CEO [8].

items.head: Schneider pairs air and liquid
items.text: Schneider Electric's new coolant distribution unit combines fan-wall air cooling with liquid cooling, at up to 3.5 MW of cooling per unit [9].

items.head: An automotive supplier enters the hall
items.text: Valeo said it would present, with OVHcloud, an aluminium heat exchanger delivering a 38% increase in cooling capacity at the OCP Global Summit [10].

sections.name: 800 V DC Distribution Reaches the Cooling Plant
sections.intro: The move to high-voltage DC began at the rack. In this window it reached the mechanical plant.

items.head: Leaving 48 volts behind
items.text: As of mid-2026, the guide reports, the industry is converging on 800 V DC as the reference voltage for power distribution, with NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft jointly advancing the architecture through the Open Compute Project [14].

items.head: A chiller on 800 V DC
items.text: Trane Technologies, with Eaton and Danfoss, demonstrated a chiller operating directly from an 800 V DC feed, delivering more than 3.5 MW of cooling and up to 2% higher efficiency [15].

items.head: What 800 V DC means for cooling
items.text: Schneider Electric's Mike Donahue discussed 800 V DC and its implications for data center cooling as AI workloads raise rack power density [16].

items.head: One reference design for heat and power
items.text: Trane Technologies and Eaton developed an integrated reference design for high-density data centers that combines thermal management and power systems [17].

items.head: Densities of 200 to 300 kW
items.text: Schneider Electric writes that as rack densities rise to 200–300 kW and beyond, cooling capacity has become a critical requirement [11].

sections.name: Power Conversion, Switchgear & Storage
sections.intro: Behind the new voltage sits a supply chain of semiconductors, transformers and switchgear. The period brought reference designs, acquisitions and factory expansions across it.

items.head: Direct 800 V to 6 V conversion
items.text: Navitas Semiconductor and Microchip unveiled a 20 kW reference design for direct 800 V to 6 V DC conversion using GaN devices, targeting 96% peak efficiency and 2,100 W/in³ [18].

items.head: Infineon completes C2i
items.text: Infineon completed its acquisition of C2i Semiconductors, a Bengaluru company specialising in digital power management and multiphase controllers for AI data centers [19].

items.head: Eaton buys medium-voltage capacity
items.text: Eaton agreed to acquire Italy-based COL Group for €810 million to strengthen its medium-voltage capabilities in Europe [20].

items.head: Software-defined switchgear
items.text: Schneider Electric is extending software-defined architecture into the medium-voltage layer of AI data centers with a standardized switchgear platform [21].

items.head: Flex values Axiom at $37.5 billion
items.text: Flex secured a $2.0 billion convertible preferred investment in Axiom Solutions International from General Catalyst, Koch Equity Development and co-investors, valuing the AI infrastructure spin-off at $37.5 billion enterprise value [22].

items.head: Hyosung expands in Memphis
items.text: Hyosung is investing $300 million in Memphis transformer manufacturing, with capacity expansion of more than 50% by 2028 [23].

items.head: Generator to chip
items.text: Wärtsilä, Schneider Electric and Stanley Consultants launched a coordinated approach integrating onsite generation, electrical infrastructure and engineering [24].

items.head: LG's battery system qualifies
items.text: LG Energy Solution's 2.5 MW / 5.1 MWh battery energy storage system achieved NVIDIA DSX Ready qualification [25].

items.head: Three battery makers named
items.text: Nvidia launched a battery storage qualification program for AI data centers, initially naming Tesla, LG and Hitachi [26].

sections.name: Water, Siting & the Control Layer
sections.intro: The thermal choice now reaches beyond the hall, into water budgets, local approvals and the software that runs both systems together.

items.head: Electricity and water, by the numbers
items.text: Citing the IEA, the report puts global data center electricity use at 485 TWh in 2025, up 17%, and Google's water use up 34% to 10.9 billion gallons [27].

items.head: Cooling design and community opposition
items.text: A Motivair executive writes that community opposition and local approvals are becoming bigger constraints on capacity, and that cooling design affects water, noise and permitting [12].

items.head: Recycled water in India
items.text: The post notes India has around 18% of the world's population but only 4% of its freshwater resources [28].

items.head: Thermal orchestration
items.text: The article argues that workload, flow, pressure, coolant chemistry and facility heat rejection now move together in high-density racks and need an orchestration layer [13].

items.head: Digital twins for power and cooling
items.text: The report records Vertiv's SmartRun digital twin progress within NVIDIA Omniverse DSX for coordinated power-cooling simulation, and an NTT DATA–Daikin validation of AI that predicts server thermal conditions [29].

items.head: DCIM market forecast
items.text: MarketsandMarkets projects the DCIM market will reach $8.42 billion by 2031 [30].

take: The cited record shows vendors from opposite sides of the hall entering each other's line of business: a chiller maker running on the power vendor's DC bus [15], a power vendor shipping coolant distribution units [9], and an integrated reference design from both [17]. NVIDIA's qualification sits above all of them [1, 2, 5, 25]. Read together, the evidence suggests buyers will specify one heat-and-power system against NVIDIA's reference architecture, and that a vendor offering only one half will compete for the subcontract rather than the contract.
method: Source rule: every factual sentence carries a numbered citation to a Faraday Signal (Supabase public.signals) or crawled artifact (public.artifacts); each records the publisher URL below. Sentences restate the recorded framing or summary, using only complete clauses where the record was truncated. Nothing comes from the retired Gamma deck or from model memory.

Selection: Signals and artifacts tagged D7.1–D7.4, D2.1, D2.3, D2.4 and D2.10, dated 8 Sep–12 Oct 2026, filtered for cooling and power-conversion terms, de-duplicated, Google News redirects excluded, then curated by hand. Items mis-tagged to these Threads (chip smuggling, optics, storage) were dropped. Vendor blogs are cited as the vendor's own statement.
Limits: primary articles were not re-fetched for this sample. Faraday's Take is analysis of the cited items and adds no facts. Status: draft, not signed off (Brand Bible §07).
